body.text: In the weeks leading up to this year’s midterm elections, one of the few legislative bright spots in an anaemic Washington has been AI regulation.

The Trump administration has been wary of touching an industry it sees as vital in America’s great-power competition with China, each side seeing any advantage gained by the other as evidence of impending doom. Meanwhile, though, public pressure has begun to mount.

News that a growing majority of Americans — 73 per cent at last count — are concerned about the threats posed by AI has spurred legislators in both parties to begin negotiating. Republicans have been reluctant to pass legislation that Trump would find unpalatable, but Democrats are increasingly pondering regulation Trump might be persuaded to sign off on if they win control of Congress.

The question comes at a time when the political winds are shifting. The rightward political realignment that many, including the largest AI firms, assumed was inevitable after Trump’s 2024 election is coming undone. That too might affect the conditions under which Trump, Congress or the AI industry make their next decisions. The upshot is that AI regulation seems poised to take centre stage in 2027.

Democrats and Republicans will both be looking to show the American public they can govern for the future. Presidential candidates will be on the trail outlining their vision of how the next administration should approach the issue. The beginnings of these moves are already in place.

In the Senate, bipartisan negotiations have been led by Democratic senator Amy Klobuchar and Republican senator John Thune, though they have stalled as the midterms approach. A proposal by senator Maria Cantwell, a former tech executive, would allow government experts to set safety standards and inspect AI models before their public release.

In the House, the Democrats’ Lori Trahan and the Republicans’ Jay Obernolte have recently introduced the next iteration of a bill that would see heavier regulatory burdens placed on leading AI companies. Although it’s unlikely to pass as it is, it offers a view of what a bipartisan compromise might look like: independent verification, clear reporting requirements, risk management plans and government capacity to intervene in an emergency.

Where we’ve arrived is an agreement that AI needs governing rather than a deal over how to govern it. The major disagreement is about where the point of control should be. Should companies be able to regulate themselves or should government play a more active role? It matters who writes and evaluates the standards, and whether public institutions can stop a model from being released.

Next week’s midterms won’t change everything. Democratic control of the House will mean a new focus on investigations and political agenda-setting. If Democrats take the Senate, they will have greater control over who Trump can put in certain roles. But they won’t overtake the executive.

What Democrats do stand to gain in this election is more power to expose and challenge the AI industry’s relationship with Washington. In the most recent chapter of Silicon Valley–Washington relations, any perceived distance between the two has been erased.

For generations, rivalry kept the companies and the administration independent of one another, allowing American technology to become the basis for much of the world’s communication. Other countries could trust American technology — unlike Chinese tech — because it was not seen as an arm of the state’s political project.
Now, technological progress is a proxy for national interest. Republicans in particular have embraced the idea that America’s competition with China will be on the fields of AI.
That interlocking of interests has been helpful both to the Republican Party and to the AI industry, at least for a while. But most Americans don’t see the AI industry in that way.

The last time America saw itself in a national technological battle for supremacy, president John F. Kennedy called on the nation to race to the moon. The technology and its object felt far away and ambitious. Its development had little effect on daily lives other than the swell of pride when the flag was planted on the moon.

Now, 57 per cent of Americans consider AI to be bad for society, 66 per cent oppose data centre construction, and 67 per cent oppose how Trump is handling AI. Where AI executives talk about technological challenges, everyday people worry about jobs, bills, their children’s education and how their communities are being transformed by a technology they barely understand.

Republicans pitch more AI as a weapon in the competition with China — a burden they are being asked to bear in the interests of great-power rivalry. But are ordinary Americans happy to take up that burden? The answer seems to be no. A poll last month revealed that 85 per cent of registered voters preferred cooperation with China on AI to the push to develop American AI as fast as possible.

If Democrats gain control of the investigative functions of Congress they will attempt to turn hearings into decisive moments. Public anxiety gains a voice when the megarich villains of the popular imagination are forced to reveal what they knew, which safeguards they ignored, and how much they have benefited from the public’s confusion.

These are entirely different concerns from the issues both parties’ regulatory bills have so far dealt with. On its own, an independent capacity to audit AI models will do nothing to ease the anxiety constituents feel over rising electricity costs.

The post-midterm congressional hearings will coincide with the manoeuvring by potential candidates that precedes the presidential primaries. AI regulation will undoubtedly be an issue, and holding the AI industry accountable will be a profitable seam for Democratic candidates to mine. After all, AI companies have no natural constituency. No one is ready to come to their defence. Sometimes the right targets are the easy targets.

The last two years of unified Republican control in Washington have seen how quickly the technology can develop. Democratic opposition with some degree of congressional power will look to give everyday Americans a role in consenting to that process. The terms of that consent will create problems for the companies that have staked their future, and the trillions of dollars in economic growth tied to it, on an open path ahead of them.

After Donald Trump’s victory in 2024, it seemed like his political project would reshape American politics. Silicon Valley quickly aligned with the administration, ostensibly to use the power of the US government to prevent foreign governments from limiting what Silicon Valley could do.

That bid was successful. The Trump administration has used the weight of government to supply AI companies with massive government contracts that have underwritten commercial growth, and it applied diplomatic pressure primarily against allies and partners to prevent them from regulating AI. A Trump spokesperson went so far as to call Australia’s recent “digital duty of care” proposals “extortion,” likening any attempt to regulate American AI to a threat against the nation itself.

Much has been made of Silicon Valley’s rightward shift. To call it an ideological move would be to presume that Silicon Valley has a social or moral ideology beyond the preservation of its own capacity for enrichment. There is a longstanding belief among that particular crowd that any restriction of their own genius will be to the detriment of society as a whole.

This is best typified by tech investor Peter Thiel’s notorious 2025 lecture, in which he called anyone who attempted to slow the progress of technology “the Antichrist.” The Pope himself was moved to rebut that argument.

Historically, Silicon Valley had kept its distance from Washington, understanding that constantly changing winds may leave it exposed. Now, after lashing itself to Trump in the hope of a great leap forward, the winds are again shifting.

Trump’s political project is no longer popular, even among his own voters. Companies are nervous that the future they’ve invested so heavily in may no longer materialise. As the Washington Post recently reported, many of these firms are preparing for congressional investigations and trying to hire Democratic insiders to insulate themselves from the danger ahead.

Not all companies are taking the same path. OpenAI leads a coalition of companies trying to hold the Trump-era regulatory gap open. Anthropic is positioning itself as its chief rival commercially and politically. All the companies are deeply tied into the fabric of the Trump administration but are trying to find a way out of its grasp. The danger of a trapped animal is that it will thrash about, as we’re seeing the Trump administration do now. Those still in the cage will be hit first.

Silicon Valley is trying to preserve the benefits of the relationship it cultivated with Trump while reducing the costs of public awareness of that relationship. Neither Trump nor a public that now sees him as a liability take kindly to that approach.

So how might Trump be persuaded to support regulation? He has been loyal to AI companies because they have played a role in his political success. Unlike tariffs or draconian immigration enforcement, it is not one of his prized instinctive moves. But he may well sense a change in the national mood and use it as an opportunity to take ownership of regulation and turn it into an applause line.

It’s plausible that Trump could accept a deal that protects a loosely defined free hand for “innovation” as a cudgel against China while accepting visible but limited constraints on the industry. What’s unclear is whether Democrats will be willing to accept that deal or would rather wait for the possibility of a Democratic president to sign a better deal in 2029.

While countries like Australia can do quite a lot to contest the power of these companies within their own borders, they have little influence over the actual development of the technology or the global capabilities the companies possess. Other middle powers are also beginning to question the degree to which these companies and their technologies are now an extension of Trump’s political project globally.

Brazil offers a glimpse. In the last two weeks of the second round of the presidential election that saw the return of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva for a fourth term, Meta employees acknowledged that their own systems disadvantaged Lula in favour of the right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro (though the company disputes any intent). Bolsonaro, who was supported by Trump, was offered exile in Florida in the days after his defeat. The result was deep distrust among the Brazilian public about the role of American technology, with majorities deeply concerned about American influence in their politics as a result.

How the next Congress attempts to regulate and constrain the AI industry will matter as Australia, Brazil and the rest of the world contemplate both how to regulate the technology they already have, and whether to look for alternatives they can trust. After the new Congress gets under way in January we’ll begin finding out whether the most powerful democracy in the world can still exercise meaningful control over technologies that grab at the loose threads of democratic society. •
